marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q001.takeaway: Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is secreted by salivary glands and begins starch digestion in the mouth.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q001.displayText:
Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is secreted by salivary glands and begins starch digestion in the mouth.

Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is secreted by the salivary gland.

There are 3 pairs of salivary glands:
• Parotid
• Submandibular
• Sublingual glands

Functions of saliva are summarized in the source figure.
emphasis: Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is secreted by salivary glands and begins starch digestion in the mouth

rationales.a: Gastric glands secrete acid, pepsinogen and intrinsic factor, not ptyalin.
rationales.b: Duodenal Brunner glands secrete alkaline mucus, not salivary amylase.
rationales.d: Pancreas secretes pancreatic amylase, which is distinct from salivary ptyalin.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q002.takeaway: The muscularis mucosa causes local mucosal movement; peristalsis is generated mainly by muscularis externa, so the statement is false.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q002.displayText:
The muscularis mucosa causes local mucosal movement; peristalsis is generated mainly by muscularis externa, so the statement is false.

Muscularis propria is associated with peristalsis and not muscularis mucosa. Contraction of muscularis mucosa alters absorptive and secretive surface area.

Meissner’s plexus (submucosal plexus) is present in the submucosa. The myenteric plexus (Auerbach plexus) is present between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layer.

Villi are absent in the large intestine but present in the small intestine.

Layers of intestinal wall from outside to inside are:
• Serosa
• Longitudinal smooth muscle layer
• Circular smooth muscle layer
• Submucosa
• Mucosa
emphasis: The muscularis mucosa causes local mucosal movement; peristalsis is generated mainly by muscularis externa, so the statement is false

rationales.a: Meissner (submucosal) plexus lies in the submucosa.
rationales.b: Auerbach (myenteric) plexus lies between circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
rationales.d: Large intestine lacks villi, although it has crypts.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q003.takeaway: Salivary amylase is inactivated by the acidic pH of the stomach.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q003.displayText:
Salivary amylase is inactivated by the acidic pH of the stomach.

Salivary amylase is inactivated by the low pH of the stomach. It is rapidly denatured at pH 4 (gastric pH is 1 to 3.5). Salivary amylase is activated by chloride.

Salivary α-amylase (Ptyalin):
• Digests starch: cleaves internal α-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch
• Optimum pH: 7
• Denatured at pH 4

Since a large portion of a meal often remains unmixed for a considerable length of time in the stomach, the salivary enzyme may account for digestion of as much as 75% of the starch present before it is denatured by gastric acid.

Note: Even in the absence of salivary amylase, there is no defect in carbohydrate digestion because pancreatic amylase is sufficient to digest all of the ingested starch.
emphasis: Salivary amylase is inactivated by the acidic pH of the stomach

rationales.a: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen; it does not inactivate amylase.
rationales.c: Small-intestinal pH is neutral to alkaline and permits pancreatic enzyme action.
rationales.d: Chloride can support salivary amylase activity rather than inactivate it.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q004.takeaway: Lingual lipase is secreted by serous glands of von Ebner near circumvallate papillae.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q004.displayText:
Lingual lipase is secreted by serous glands of von Ebner near circumvallate papillae.

Lingual lipase is secreted by von Ebner’s gland.

von Ebner’s gland is a serous salivary gland situated around circumvallate and foliate papillae in front of the terminal sulcus.

Lingual lipase hydrolyses dietary lipid. The optimal pH is 3-6. Unlike pancreatic lipase, it is not inhibited by bile salts, medium-chain FA, and lecithin. Hence, it remains active through the stomach and into the intestine.
emphasis: Lingual lipase is secreted by serous glands of von Ebner near circumvallate papillae

rationales.a: Parotid glands produce watery saliva rich in amylase, not lingual lipase.
rationales.c: Sublingual glands are mainly mucous salivary glands.
rationales.d: Submandibular glands produce mixed saliva, not the lingual lipase source.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q005.takeaway: Saliva has the highest daily potassium secretion among the listed digestive fluids.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q005.displayText:
Saliva has the highest daily potassium secretion among the listed digestive fluids.

The highest daily secretion of K+ is into the saliva.

In the process of formation of saliva, Na+ and Cl- are reabsorbed from the saliva, and K+ and HCO3- are secreted into the saliva.

Note: The highest concentration of K+ is in the rectal fluid.
emphasis: Saliva has the highest daily potassium secretion among the listed digestive fluids

rationales.a: Bile contains electrolytes but is not the highest daily K⁺ output listed.
rationales.b: Pancreatic juice contains potassium but less total daily potassium than saliva in this comparison.
rationales.c: Jejunal secretion is not the highest daily potassium source among the options.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q006.takeaway: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to parotid synapse in the otic ganglion before reaching the gland.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q006.displayText:
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to parotid synapse in the otic ganglion before reaching the gland.

The secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland pass through the Otic ganglion.

Salivary secretion is almost entirely controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system. Volume is mainly mediated by parasympathetic stimulation, while the composition of saliva (increased proteinaceous content) is slightly modified by sympathetic input.

The parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are delivered by the glossopharyngeal and facial nerves to otic and submandibular ganglia respectively.
emphasis: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to parotid synapse in the otic ganglion before reaching the gland

rationales.a: Geniculate ganglion contains sensory cell bodies of facial nerve, not the parotid secretomotor synapse.
rationales.b: Sphenopalatine ganglion supplies lacrimal and nasal glands.
rationales.d: The relevant ganglion is otic; “lesser ganglion” is not the parotid secretomotor relay.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q007.takeaway: Rennin (chymosin), the milk-curdling enzyme in infants, is found in gastric juice.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q007.displayText:
Rennin (chymosin), the milk-curdling enzyme in infants, is found in gastric juice.

Rennin is present in the gastric juice. It is also called chymosin.

It is a protein-digesting enzyme (endopeptidase) found in the stomach of newborn cows. It transforms (curdles) caseinogen into insoluble casein.

In humans and in some animals that lack rennin, milk is coagulated by the action of pepsin.

Note: Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, which hydrolyzes angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
emphasis: Rennin (chymosin), the milk-curdling enzyme in infants, is found in gastric juice

rationales.b: Pancreatic secretions contain proteases and lipase but not gastric rennin.
rationales.c: Kidney is not the digestive source of rennin.
rationales.d: Saliva contains amylase and lingual lipase, not gastric rennin.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q008.takeaway: Parietal-cell loss causes achlorhydria and intrinsic-factor deficiency, leading to pernicious anemia.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q008.displayText:
Parietal-cell loss causes achlorhydria and intrinsic-factor deficiency, leading to pernicious anemia.

Pernicious anemia develops due to autoimmune damage to the parietal cells in gastric glands.

The parietal cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor. Therefore, when the parietal cells are destroyed, both achlorhydria, as well as pernicious anemia, develop.

Pernicious anemia occurs due to deficiency of the intrinsic factor of Castle, which is important for the absorption of vitamin B12.
emphasis: Parietal-cell loss causes achlorhydria and intrinsic-factor deficiency, leading to pernicious anemia

rationales.a: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not intrinsic factor.
rationales.c: Enterochromaffin-like cells release histamine; they are not the intrinsic-factor source.
rationales.d: Goblet cells secrete mucus and do not cause pernicious anemia when lost.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q009.takeaway: Goblet cells secrete protective mucus along gastrointestinal epithelium.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q009.displayText:
Goblet cells secrete protective mucus along gastrointestinal epithelium.

Goblet cells secrete mucus. These cells are located on the surface of the crypts of Lieberkuhn and the villi of the small intestine.

Cells present in the crypts of Lieberkuhn:
• Goblet cells - secrete mucus that acts as a lubricant and protects the intestinal surface
• Epithelial cells - secrete succus entericus (intestinal secretion)
• Paneth cells - secrete lysozymes and defensins (antibacterial substances)
emphasis: Goblet cells secrete protective mucus along gastrointestinal epithelium

rationales.a: HCl is secreted by gastric parietal cells.
rationales.c: Pepsinogen is secreted by chief cells and activated to pepsin.
rationales.d: Serotonin is produced by enterochromaffin cells, not goblet cells.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q010.takeaway: Gastric parietal cells secrete H⁺ through the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, exchanging luminal H⁺ for K⁺.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q010.displayText:
Gastric parietal cells secrete H⁺ through the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, exchanging luminal H⁺ for K⁺.

H+ ions are secreted into the lumen of the stomach in exchange for K+ by the H+-K+ pump (H+, K+-ATPase).

Mechanism of HCl formation:
• In the parietal cells, CO2 and H2O are converted to H+ and HCO3-, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase.
• H+ is secreted into the lumen of the stomach by the H+-K+ pump in exchange for K+.
• HCO3- moves out of the cell into the bloodstream in exchange for Cl- (Cl-/HCO3- exchange). This Cl- moves into the lumen of the stomach.
• H+ and Cl- combine to form HCl.

As HCO3- is added to the venous blood, the pH of the blood increases. This is called alkaline tide. Eventually, this HCO3- will be secreted in the pancreatic secretions to neutralize H+ in the small intestine.

Proton pump inhibitors inhibit the H+-K+ pump.
emphasis: Gastric parietal cells secrete H⁺ through the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, exchanging luminal H⁺ for K⁺

rationales.a: Na⁺ is not the counterion exchanged by the gastric proton pump.
rationales.c: Calcium is not exchanged by the parietal-cell apical H⁺/K⁺ pump.
rationales.d: Chloride follows H⁺ into the lumen but is not the ion exchanged at the pump.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q011.takeaway: Histamine, acetylcholine and gastrin stimulate acid secretion; luminal HCl provides negative feedback and is the exception.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q011.displayText:
Histamine, acetylcholine and gastrin stimulate acid secretion; luminal HCl provides negative feedback and is the exception.

Gastric secretion is not increased by HCl. HCl decreases gastric secretion via a negative feedback mechanism.

Low pH due to HCl in the stomach inhibits gastrin secretion, which in turn inhibits H+ secretion. Hence, the presence of HCl inhibits gastric secretion.

Stimuli that increase acid and gastrin secretion:
• Distension of stomach
• Peptides
• Calcium
• Alcohol and caffeine
• Increased vagal discharge

Stimuli that decrease acid and gastrin secretion:
• Gastric acid
• Secretin family - secretin, glucagon, VIP, GIP
• Somatostatin
• CCK, Calcitonin
• PGE2
emphasis: Histamine, acetylcholine and gastrin stimulate acid secretion; luminal HCl provides negative feedback and is the exception

rationales.a: Histamine activates H₂ receptors on parietal cells and increases acid secretion.
rationales.b: Acetylcholine stimulates parietal and ECL cells.
rationales.c: Gastrin promotes acid secretion directly and through histamine release.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q012.takeaway: Somatostatin inhibits gastrin release and parietal-cell acid secretion, countering Zollinger–Ellison hypersecretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q012.displayText:
Somatostatin inhibits gastrin release and parietal-cell acid secretion, countering Zollinger–Ellison hypersecretion.

Gastric secretion is inhibited by somatostatin.

It inhibits gastric secretion via both direct and indirect pathways:
• Direct pathway - somatostatin acts directly on the acid-producing parietal cells by binding to receptors on parietal cells that are coupled to adenylyl cyclase via a Gi protein. This inhibits adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP levels are reduced. In this way, somatostatin antagonizes the stimulatory effect of histamine on H+ secretion.
• Indirect pathway - somatostatin inhibits the release of histamine and gastrin and thus decreases H+ secretion indirectly.
emphasis: Somatostatin inhibits gastrin release and parietal-cell acid secretion, countering Zollinger–Ellison hypersecretion

rationales.b: Histamine stimulates parietal-cell acid secretion via H₂ receptors.
rationales.c: Vagal stimulation increases acid secretion through acetylcholine and gastrin pathways.
rationales.d: Gastrin drives acid secretion and is elevated in Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q013.takeaway: The gastric phase produces the greatest gastric secretion, stimulated by distension, peptides and vagovagal reflexes.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q013.displayText:
The gastric phase produces the greatest gastric secretion, stimulated by distension, peptides and vagovagal reflexes.

Maximum gastric secretion occurs in the gastric phase.
emphasis: The gastric phase produces the greatest gastric secretion, stimulated by distension, peptides and vagovagal reflexes

rationales.a: The cephalic phase prepares secretion before food enters the stomach but contributes less overall.
rationales.c: The intestinal phase is generally inhibitory and contributes less gastric secretion.
rationales.d: Secretion differs across phases; gastric phase is the largest.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q014.takeaway: Gastrin from antral G cells stimulates gastric HCl secretion, directly and through ECL-cell histamine.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q014.displayText:
Gastrin from antral G cells stimulates gastric HCl secretion, directly and through ECL-cell histamine.

HCl secretion in the gastric phase is increased by gastrin.

Gastrin stimulates H+ secretion by interaction with cholecystokinin B (CCKB) receptor on the parietal cell which secretes HCl.
emphasis: Gastrin from antral G cells stimulates gastric HCl secretion, directly and through ECL-cell histamine

rationales.a: Pepsinogen is an enzyme precursor and does not stimulate acid secretion as a hormone.
rationales.b: CCK mainly regulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction.
rationales.d: Secretin inhibits gastric acid and promotes pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q015.takeaway: Exocrine pancreatic secretion is isotonic and is stimulated by CCK, especially for enzyme-rich acinar output.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q015.displayText:
Exocrine pancreatic secretion is isotonic and is stimulated by CCK, especially for enzyme-rich acinar output.

Pancreatic secretion is stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK) and Ach. It is always isotonic.

It has virtually the same Na+ and K+ concentrations as in plasma. It is rich in several digestive enzymes like amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase, elastase, etc.
emphasis: Exocrine pancreatic secretion is isotonic and is stimulated by CCK, especially for enzyme-rich acinar output

rationales.a: The source explicitly states pancreatic secretion is always isotonic, so this option is also true; the item has more than one correct answer despite the printed CCK key.
rationales.b: Acetylcholine stimulates pancreatic acinar secretion rather than inhibiting it.
rationales.c: Pancreatic secretion is isotonic, not hypotonic.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q016.takeaway: Secretin released by duodenal S cells stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic ductal secretion in response to acid.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q016.displayText:
Secretin released by duodenal S cells stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic ductal secretion in response to acid.

Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice is secreted under the influence of secretin.

Secretin is secreted by the S cells of the duodenum. Its primary function is to promote the secretion of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice by the ductal cells of the pancreas and duodenum. This secretion is poor in enzymes.

Other functions:
• Augments the effects of CCK
• Inhibits gastrin release
• Decreases gastric acid secretion
• Contraction of the pyloric sphincter
• Exerts trophic effect on the pancreas
emphasis: Secretin released by duodenal S cells stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic ductal secretion in response to acid

rationales.b: GIP primarily stimulates insulin and inhibits gastric activity; it is not the main bicarbonate stimulus.
rationales.c: Pancreatozymin is an older name for CCK, which mainly stimulates enzyme secretion.
rationales.d: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion, not pancreatic bicarbonate output.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q017.takeaway: Brunner glands secrete highly alkaline mucus that neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q017.displayText:
Brunner glands secrete highly alkaline mucus that neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

The most alkaline secretion is Brunner’s gland secretion with a pH of 8.0-8.9.

Brunner’s gland is located in the first few centimeters of the duodenal wall. It secretes large amounts of alkaline mucus in response to tactile stimuli on the duodenal mucosa, vagal stimulation, and GI hormones, especially secretin. It is inhibited by sympathetic stimulation.

The function of the mucus secreted by Brunner’s glands is to protect the duodenal wall from digestion by the highly acidic gastric juice emptying from the stomach.

Note: The second most alkaline secretion in the GI tract is the pancreatic juice.
emphasis: Brunner glands secrete highly alkaline mucus that neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum

rationales.a: Saliva is alkaline but less alkaline than Brunner gland secretion in this comparison.
rationales.d: Small-intestinal secretion is alkaline but Brunner gland secretion is most alkaline here.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q018.takeaway: Bile salts returning through enterohepatic circulation are the strongest choleretic, stimulating further bile secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH31_Q018.displayText:
Bile salts returning through enterohepatic circulation are the strongest choleretic, stimulating further bile secretion.

Bile salts (chemical choleretic) are the most potent choleretics.

Any substance that increases bile secretion is called a choleretic. Bile secretion may be increased by chemical (bile salts), hormonal (Secretin), and neural (vagal stimulation) mechanisms.

Note: Cholagogues cause contraction of the gallbladder. Eg. CCK.
emphasis: Bile salts returning through enterohepatic circulation are the strongest choleretic, stimulating further bile secretion

rationales.a: CCK mainly contracts gallbladder and relaxes sphincter of Oddi; it is not the strongest choleretic.
rationales.b: Fatty acids stimulate CCK and bile delivery but are not the direct most potent choleretic.
rationales.d: Pancreatic juice is not a stimulus for hepatic bile secretion.
